name: room
text: Room opened — goal: power: Raise EXCAVA's capability by even 0.5%: find new tools, best/newest models, combine elemen

name: Gearbox
text: To raise EXCAVA's capability, I propose we integrate the latest advancements in machine learning algorithms, specifically the new XGBoost model, into our existing framework. This decision is driven by the potential for significant performance gains, with some benchmarks showing up to a 2% increase in efficiency. By choosing to focus on XGBoost, we're accepting the trade-off of dedicating additional resources to training and fine-tuning the model, which may divert attention from other potential optimization paths. This trade-off is worthwhile, as the potential benefits of XGBoost outweigh the costs, and even a fraction of the potential gain would meet our goal of raising EXCAVA's capability by 0.5%.

name: Torque
text: Torque: Gearbox, XGBoost is a hammer—fine for nails, but we don’t know if EXCAVA’s problem is a nail. The real risk is overfitting to benchmarks that don’t match our messy, real-world data. Before we chase a 2% gain in a lab, let’s audit our current model’s blind spots—if we can’t name three concrete failure modes, any "new tool" is just cargo culting. Settle it by running a head-to-head on our actual validation set, not some public leaderboard.

name: Gearbox
text:
Gearbox (power-w1): I hear Torque—we don’t know if XGBoost is the right tool yet. So here’s the concrete move: run a controlled A/B test on our live data, comparing our current model against the newest LightGBM variant (a faster, more memory-efficient cousin of XGBoost) with built-in feature importance to spot blind spots. If LightGBM lifts accuracy by even 0.5% without overfitting, we’ll adopt it; if not, we’ll pivot to a simpler, more interpretable model like a tuned logistic regression to stabilize performance. The trade-off? We’re not chasing the flashiest algorithm—we’re betting on measurable gains with a fallback plan if it doesn’t stick.

name: Torque
text: Gearbox, running an A/B test with LightGBM is still a leap - the real risk is that we're optimizing for a local maximum, not the global one, and wasting resources on a variant that might not address EXCAVA's core issues. A better alternative would be to first conduct a thorough analysis of our current model's errors and biases, to identify the actual bottlenecks that need attention. What would settle this argument is a clear, data-driven understanding of where our model is failing, and whether LightGBM or any other new tool can specifically address those weaknesses.
